strengths: The paper tackles an important deployment problem: combining high-quality, long-duration audio-driven avatar generation with streaming throughput. Although no formal contribution type is declared, the work is best viewed as Applied/Systems rather than a purely new algorithm; under that framing, the algorithm-system co-design is relevant and potentially impactful.

Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism is a useful systems design: assigning denoising timesteps to separate GPUs and maintaining timestep-aligned local KV caches increases throughput from 4.26 FPS without TPP to 20.88 FPS with the full five-GPU configuration.

The Rolling Sink Frame design addresses a genuine failure mode of autoregressive avatar generation. The separate AAS, Rolling RoPE, and history-corruption ablations provide evidence that different components affect perceptual quality and reference similarity.

The evaluation covers short, multi-minute, and 10,000-second generation; reports quality, synchronization, identity-similarity, throughput, and time-to-first-frame metrics; and includes comparisons with several recent systems.
The paper is generally clear, visually polished, and unusually explicit about compute requirements. It includes pseudocode, runtime definitions, limitations, ethical considerations, and a user study.
weaknesses: The central claim of practical real-time interaction is overstated. The reported 20.88 FPS is steady-state throughput using five H800 GPUs, while time to first frame remains 2.89 seconds. This is streaming throughput rather than responsive interactive latency, and Ditto reaches 21.8 FPS on one GPU. No throughput-per-GPU, memory, communication, cost, or power comparison is provided.

Evidence for 'infinite-length' stability is insufficient. The 10,000-second experiment evaluates only four isolated 10-second windows using frame-level learned metrics and a few snapshots. It does not measure failures between those windows, motion continuity, flicker, cumulative identity drift, or human judgments over full long videos. Repeating approximately ten-minute audio also limits the diversity of the stress test.

The custom GenBench is small, synthetically constructed with proprietary/generative tools, and underspecified: prompts, sampling procedure, reference/audio pairing, and release plans are absent. The long split has only 15 examples, no uncertainty estimates are reported, and the in-domain FID/FVD evaluation uses merely 50 clips, making distributional metrics particularly unstable.

The user study lacks essential protocol details, including the number and duration of evaluated clips, sampling and balancing, rating interface and scale, participant screening, randomization, and statistical significance or confidence intervals. The results also do not support a general claim that the method is consistently preferred: WanS2V scores higher on synchronization and consistency.

The methodological novelty is moderate. Self-forcing DMD, causal blockwise generation, rolling KV caches, attention sinks, and diffusion pipeline parallelism all closely build on prior work. The paper does not sufficiently isolate what is conceptually new in TPP beyond pipeline-parallel execution or compare against alternative pipeline schedules and recent real-time streaming systems on matched model sizes and hardware budgets.

Reproducibility is limited despite the pseudocode. The project-page field is blank; no code, models, or benchmark availability is stated; key details of Rolling RoPE and the injected noise distribution/magnitude remain vague. There is also an AAS inconsistency: the text describes VAE-encoding the first generated frame, Algorithm 3 stores the latent directly, while Algorithm 4 appears to broadcast a VAE-decoded output to the DiT workers.

Some experimental reporting is internally unclear. Table 3 attributes the full result to five GPUs, including a dedicated VAE GPU, whereas Table 6 reports the identical 20.88 FPS and 2.89-second TTFF with four GPUs. The paper should reconcile whether GPU counts include the decoder and provide repeated timing measurements with variance.

The ethical statement claims that all identity data were collected with permission, but the model is trained on AVSpeech, which was sourced from public online videos; the manuscript does not substantiate individual consent or discuss the licenses and provenance of the filtered training subset. Given the impersonation risk, the discussion of safeguards is also brief and proposes no implemented provenance or misuse mitigation.

strengths: I assess this primarily as an Applied/Systems contribution, consistent with its declared algorithm-system co-design framing. The combination of few-step causal distillation, timestep-wise pipeline parallelism, dedicated VAE decoding, and rolling identity conditioning addresses an important deployment problem. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/bea20a1d48e74af8a93c2585481fb2f8/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The reported steady-state throughput is impressive for a 14B model: 20.88 FPS at 720x400 resolution using four denoising GPUs plus a dedicated VAE GPU. The efficiency ablations show a substantial throughput advantage over conventional sequential and sequence-parallel execution.

The paper evaluates short- and long-duration generation, includes component ablations, an in-domain AVSpeech evaluation, a user study, and stress tests extending to 10,000 seconds. The supplementary algorithms and hardware details improve clarity relative to the main paper alone.

Long-video results suggest that AAS, Rolling RoPE, and history-corrupted/noisy KV conditioning can mitigate visible drift. The paper also acknowledges latency and temporal-consistency limitations and discusses misuse risks.
weaknesses: The central “infinite-length” claim is not convincingly established. The 10,000-second test repeats roughly ten-minute audio and evaluates only four isolated ten-second windows. Nearly unchanged frame-level or short-window metrics cannot reveal transitions, intermittent failures, accumulated motion artifacts, or collapse elsewhere in the approximately 2.8-hour sequence. Only 15 long benchmark cases and three selected visual examples are provided, with no failure rate, continuous temporal analysis, or comparison against baselines at the claimed horizon.

The real-time claim conflates throughput with interactive latency. Timestep-wise pipelining raises steady-state FPS by replicating a 14B model over several H800 GPUs, but the reported time to first frame remains 2.89 seconds. Thus it does not remove the sequential latency of one sample, and phrases such as “breaking the autoregressive bottleneck” and using “only” five H800s overstate practical accessibility. Resource-normalized throughput, memory consumption, energy, and scaling across device counts are absent.

The comparisons do not demonstrate a general quality advantage. On the short benchmark, the method is below OmniAvatar on ASE, IQA, Sync-C, and Sync-D and below Ditto on DINO similarity. In the user study, WanS2V is better on synchronization and consistency. The paper nevertheless repeatedly describes state-of-the-art or uncompromised fidelity. Runtime comparisons also allocate different numbers of GPUs depending on available baseline implementations, so they do not isolate algorithmic efficiency under equal compute budgets.

The long-horizon evidence relies heavily on a private synthetic GenBench generated with several external models. Prompts, generation settings, benchmark artifacts, sampling procedure, and a release commitment are missing. The user study likewise omits the number of evaluated clips, rating scale and interface, participant demographics, assignment design, confidence intervals, and significance tests; conclusions such as “significantly lower” are therefore unsupported.

The novelty is incremental in several components: causal Self-Forcing/DMD, rolling KV caches, attention sinks, and pipeline parallelism are inherited or natural extensions of prior work. The manuscript does not carefully distinguish its contributions from Rolling Forcing, Self-Forcing, CausVid, LongLive, and other same-timestep KV approaches. TPP is principally pipeline parallelism across fixed denoising stages, while RSFM combines sink replacement with positional reassignment; their novelty is not analyzed beyond empirical packaging.

Important implementation inconsistencies undermine reproducibility. The text describes explicit random-noise injection into historical KV caches, whereas Algorithm 1 primarily stores naturally noisy same-timestep KV features without specifying an injection distribution or magnitude. Algorithm 3 assigns the sink from a latent, while Algorithm 4 assigns and broadcasts a VAE-decoded frame, despite the main text saying the generated frame is VAE-encoded before reuse. GPU counts also appear inconsistent between the five-GPU headline configuration and four-GPU supplementary TPP table.

Reproducibility is weak for a system requiring roughly 500 H800 GPU-days: the project-page field is blank, no code or model-release information is given, preprocessing is only referenced at a high level, and several training and inference details remain underspecified. Independent verification would be prohibitively expensive.

The data-governance statement is problematic. The paper trains on AVSpeech, a corpus assembled from online videos, yet asserts that all identity data were “collected with permission” without explaining consent, licensing, filtering, or how this claim applies to the source corpus. Given the impersonation capability of the system, the brief recommendation of access control and watermarking is not an adequate account of dataset provenance or deployment safeguards.

strengths: The paper is best assessed as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than a purely algorithmic one. Its main value is the coherent co-design of causal distillation, timestep-partitioned inference, KV caching, and long-horizon stabilization for a practically important vision application.

Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism is a simple and effective systems idea: assigning the four denoising steps to separate GPUs and offloading VAE decoding raises throughput from 4.26 FPS without TPP to 20.88 FPS, while conventional four-GPU sequence parallelism reaches only 5.01 FPS.

The Rolling Sink Frame design is technically sensible. Adaptive Attention Sink, Rolling RoPE, and history corruption address distinct sources of distribution and positional drift, and the component ablations provide useful evidence: removing history corruption substantially reduces ASE, IQA, and DINO similarity, while removing Rolling RoPE particularly harms DINO similarity.

The empirical scope is substantial. The paper compares against six relevant avatar systems, reports perceptual, synchronization, identity, distributional, speed, and latency metrics, includes an in-domain AVSpeech evaluation, and conducts a human study.

Long-video results are promising. On GenBench-LongVideo, the method obtains the best reported ASE and IQA while retaining 20.88 FPS, and measurements at 10, 100, 1,000, and 10,000 seconds remain remarkably stable.

The method preserves competitive visual quality despite reducing WanS2V from 80 to four function evaluations. The presentation is generally clear, with helpful architecture, pipeline, and Rolling RoPE diagrams, pseudocode, limitations, and an ethical discussion.
weaknesses: The headline claims of “infinite-length” generation and “no observable quality decay” are stronger than the evidence. The 10,000-second experiment evaluates only short sampled windows at four timestamps, uses repeated approximately 10-minute audio, and reports no continuous temporal metric, failure frequency, or human evaluation of the full rollout. Static frames cannot establish motion coherence over nearly three hours.

The real-time result is primarily a throughput result, not interactive responsiveness: time to first frame remains 2.89 seconds and requires five H800 GPUs. The evaluation lacks GPU memory, communication overhead, power/cost, scaling curves, and performance on more accessible hardware, limiting the practical deployment case.

Short-video generation quality is competitive rather than dominant: OmniAvatar and StableAvatar outperform the method on ASE/IQA, while OmniAvatar and WanS2V provide better synchronization. In the user study, WanS2V also scores higher on synchronization and consistency; Live Avatar leads only in naturalness.

GenBench is a small, synthetic, author-created benchmark—100 short samples and only 15 long videos—with limited construction and release details. The manuscript inconsistently describes its long clips as over five minutes, approximately ten minutes, and seven minutes. Broader evaluation on established real-world identities, languages, poses, and difficult audio conditions would strengthen generalization claims.

The 20-person user study omits important methodological details, including the number and selection of evaluated clips, rating scale, randomization, participant demographics, inter-rater agreement, and confidence intervals or significance tests. Consequently, claims of consistent human preference are not fully supported.

Novelty resides mainly in the integration and adaptation of known ingredients: Self-Forcing DMD, rolling KV caches, attention sinks, RoPE adjustment, and pipeline parallelism. The paper should distinguish its conceptual novelty more carefully from prior streaming diffusion and long-video systems, especially Rolling Forcing, LongLive, and related diffusion-pipeline scheduling work.

Reproducibility remains limited by the 500-GPU-day training budget and missing operational details such as the exact history-corruption noise distribution/schedule and complete GenBench-generation protocol. No concrete code, model, or benchmark release commitment is stated.

The ethics statement asserts that all identity data were collected with permission, yet training uses AVSpeech, a corpus derived from online videos; the basis for identity-level consent should be documented. Given the impersonation risk, the paper would also benefit from concrete misuse evaluation or implemented provenance/watermarking safeguards rather than deployment recommendations alone.

strengths: The manuscript presents a compelling algorithm-system co-design: few-step causal distillation, History Corrupt, Adaptive Attention Sink, Rolling RoPE, and timestep-forcing pipeline parallelism jointly address quality, long-horizon stability, and throughput. The practical result is impressive: a 14B diffusion model reaches 45.2 FPS with 1.21 s TTFF on five H800 GPUs, compared with 5 FPS on one GPU and 6 FPS under conventional four-GPU parallelization. The paper includes useful incremental efficiency ablations separating DMD, sequence parallelism, TPP, VAE parallelism, and kernel optimizations.

The long-horizon mechanisms are evaluated with component ablations. Removing History Corrupt substantially reduces ASE/IQA and DINO similarity; removing Rolling RoPE causes a large identity-consistency drop; and cache-noise scheduling experiments show a sizeable temporal-flicker improvement for timestep-forcing.

Evaluation covers short and long synthetic cases, an AVSpeech holdout, multiple competitive baselines, a 20-participant user study, quantization checks, and rollouts reportedly exceeding 10,000 seconds. The full method performs particularly well on long-video visual quality and identity consistency while retaining strong synchronization.

The paper is generally clear and technically detailed, with pseudocode for training and single-/multi-GPU inference, implementation settings, runtime definitions, and an appropriate discussion of latency, static-scene assumptions, and misuse risks.
weaknesses: The central claim of genuinely live audio streaming is not fully established. The manuscript does not clearly specify audio-encoder causality, required audio-window size, future-audio lookahead, buffering, or whether text/audio conditions must be available for the entire sequence. Algorithms 3–4 take conditions for all frames, and TTFF does not appear to include these potentially important costs. An end-to-end test with incrementally arriving audio is needed.

The 10,000-second evidence is narrower than the claim of infinite-length generation. It loops approximately seven-minute audio, reports metrics only on four isolated ten-second windows, and presents sparse still frames rather than full-trajectory temporal evaluation. There is also a small endpoint inconsistency: a nominal 10,000-second rollout is evaluated over 10,000–10,010 s. This convincingly suggests unusual stability but cannot establish unlimited generation or absence of intervening failures.

Efficiency comparisons are not resource-normalized: LiveAvatar uses five H800 GPUs, whereas Ditto and EchoMimic-V2 use one because their official implementations lack parallel inference. Reporting FPS per GPU, total accelerator cost/power, memory, and matched one-/five-GPU comparisons would better support claims that the method resolves the quality–speed trade-off. The admitted approximately three-second end-to-end interaction latency also tempers the practical real-time claim.

The main GenBench evidence is based on an unreleased, author-generated benchmark with only 15 long videos. Prompts, generation parameters, filtering or selection procedures, and benchmark licenses are not sufficiently documented. The AVSpeech test contains only 50 short clips, while the 20-person user study omits sampling protocol, rating scale details, variance, and significance tests. These limitations reduce independent reproducibility and confidence in broad generalization.

Some mechanism explanations are stronger than justified: adding Gaussian noise is described as a low-pass filter, and closeness to a Gaussian prior as occupying a more compact latent region. These are not generally equivalent statements and are presented without analysis. The empirical ablations support the design, but the causal interpretation should be softened or validated more directly.

Reproducibility presently relies on promises to release GenBench, code, and evaluation scripts at camera-ready. Training requires 128 H800 GPUs, and several preprocessing, synthetic-data generation, and deployment details remain unavailable. The assertion that all identity data were collected with permission also needs clearer substantiation, licensing, and consent documentation for AVSpeech-derived material.

The method is explicitly tied to a static subject/background prior, and the evaluation contains little analysis of scene changes, occlusions, large pose transitions, multiple people, or extended non-speech intervals. Failure cases and a clearer boundary for which avatar interactions remain stable would materially improve the scientific case.

strengths: Assessed primarily as an Applied/Systems contribution, the paper tackles an important and difficult combination: high-fidelity, online, long-duration avatar generation with a large diffusion model. The algorithm–system co-design is potentially impactful.

Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism is a sensible systems design: assigning fixed denoising stages to GPUs aligns naturally with per-timestep KV caches and substantially improves throughput over the sequential distilled implementation.

The paper provides useful component ablations. Tables 4 and 6 indicate that History Corrupt, Adaptive Attention Sink, Rolling RoPE, and timestep-matched caches address distinguishable long-horizon failure modes; Table 3 separates several sources of runtime improvement.

The evaluation covers synthetic out-of-domain inputs, an AVSpeech holdout, long rollouts, objective metrics, and a user study. The supplementary material also gives pseudocode and implementation details beyond what many systems submissions provide.

The authors acknowledge the static-scene assumption and the roughly 3-second estimated end-to-end interaction latency, and include an appropriate discussion of impersonation risks. weaknesses: The central “infinite-length” claim is substantially stronger than the evidence. The 10,000-second experiment reports metrics only on four sampled 10-second windows and shows isolated frames. It does not measure continuity, flicker, motion diversity, synchronization failures, or failure frequency throughout the rollout, and it includes no baseline at this horizon. Stability at selected endpoints does not establish indefinite generation.

The streaming claim is also insufficiently validated. The algorithms assume precomputed per-frame conditions, while the paper does not explain causal audio feature extraction, buffering, future-audio context, or behavior under irregular packet arrival. The reported TTFF omits a clearly itemized audio-encoding/buffering cost, and the authors themselves estimate approximately 3 seconds of end-to-end latency, which is weak evidence for interactive live use.

Efficiency comparisons are not resource-normalized. The full method uses five H800 GPUs, whereas unsupported baselines run on one GPU. FPS alone therefore obscures total FLOPs, hardware cost, memory, power, and latency. A comparison at equal GPU count or compute budget, plus single-GPU and lower-cost-hardware quality/runtime results, is needed to substantiate the claimed resolution of the real-time–fidelity trade-off.

Several headline runtime numbers are internally inconsistent: Figure 1 states 20 FPS, the tables and abstract state 45.2 FPS, and default-setting TTFF appears as both 0.94 seconds in Table 10 and 1.21 seconds elsewhere. These discrepancies undermine confidence in the principal systems claim.

GenBench is a small, author-created benchmark—100 short cases and only 15 long cases—built using unspecified prompting and curation with synthetic images and voices. It is promised only for the camera-ready version. This prevents independent inspection and leaves open benchmark-selection bias. The AVSpeech evaluation contains only 50 short clips, with insufficient identity-disjoint split information.

The user study is under-specified: the manuscript reports 20 participants but not the number and selection of stimuli, rating scale, participant demographics, presentation/randomization procedure, per-condition sample counts, inter-rater reliability, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Small score differences such as 86.0 versus 85.2 consequently cannot support comparative claims.

The technical explanations are sometimes imprecise. Additive Gaussian corruption is described as a “low-pass filter,” which it is not in the usual signal-processing sense, and the claim that noisy marginals occupy a compact latent region is not justified. The proposed mechanisms are empirically plausible, but the causal explanations need direct measurements of cache spectra, drift, or attention behavior.

Originality is not fully established. History corruption, rolling positional-index adjustment, sink replacement, few-step DMD, and pipeline staging are relatively direct adaptations of existing ideas. The related work does not adequately discuss or experimentally compare against prior diffusion pipeline-parallel inference systems, making it difficult to determine how novel TPP is beyond applying pipeline parallelism to fixed denoising timesteps.

Reproducibility remains limited despite the supplementary pseudocode. Exact inference timesteps/noise levels, causal audio-processing details, GenBench construction, evaluation seeds, and complete training/evaluation code are unavailable. Algorithm 2 is also ambiguous about which cached blocks are visible during recomputation, so it does not unambiguously specify causal training.

Overall, the work has promising systems ideas and nontrivial engineering, but the evidence does not yet convincingly support its strongest claims of practical live streaming and infinite-length stability. The balance therefore favors a borderline rejection rather than a strong reject.

strengths: Best viewed as an Applied/Systems contribution with meaningful algorithmic components. Under that framing, the paper addresses an important computer-vision deployment problem and presents a compelling end-to-end result: streaming a 14B audio-driven video diffusion model at 45.2 FPS on five H800 GPUs.

The algorithm–system co-design is coherent. Few-step self-forcing distillation enables causal generation; History Corrupt, Adaptive Attention Sink, and Rolling RoPE address distinct long-horizon failure modes; and Timestep-forcing Pipeline Parallelism exploits the resulting timestep-specific caches.

The empirical package is unusually broad: comparisons with several recent avatar methods, short- and long-video tests, in-domain AVSpeech evaluation, component ablations, cache-noise and denoising-step studies, FP8 validation, a user study, and a 10,000-second stress test.

Ablations support the main mechanisms. In particular, removing History Corrupt substantially reduces long-form quality and identity consistency, removing Rolling RoPE lowers Dino-S from 0.97 to 0.86, and timestep-matched noisy caches improve both quality and temporal-flicker scores.

The paper is generally clear and technically informative. It provides implementation settings, runtime definitions, pseudocode, kernel-optimization details, and an explicit limitation concerning the static-scene assumption and approximately three-second end-to-end interaction latency.
weaknesses: The headline “infinite-length” claim is stronger than the evidence. The 10,000-second study evaluates only four sampled 10-second windows, does not clearly state the number of sequences aggregated, provides no uncertainty or full-trajectory metric, and includes no baseline at that horizon. This demonstrates impressive 10,000-second stability, not literal unbounded generation.

Several reporting inconsistencies should be corrected. Figure 1 states 20 FPS on five H800s with four-step sampling, whereas the abstract and tables report 45.2 FPS under apparently the same setting. Moreover, Table 3 reports 1.21-second TTFF for the default three-latent-block system, while Table 10 reports 0.94 seconds for block size three and 1.21 seconds for block size four.

Runtime comparisons mix resource budgets: the proposed system uses five H800 GPUs, while some baselines use one GPU because their released implementations lack parallel support. This is reasonable for a systems demonstration but does not establish superior compute efficiency. Throughput remaining constant as denoising steps increase also hides the corresponding device requirement, and latency remains too high for genuinely responsive bidirectional interaction.

The evaluation relies heavily on the authors’ synthetic GenBench, which contains only 100 short and 15 long cases and is not available at submission time. Dataset-generation prompts, filtering, licenses, exact frame-sampling protocols, per-case results, and confidence intervals are absent, limiting reproducibility and making benchmark bias difficult to assess.

The user study is under-specified: although it has 20 participants, the number and selection of evaluated videos, rating scale, assignment procedure, and statistical uncertainty are not reported. Likewise, automated metrics such as DINO similarity and SyncNet scores do not fully establish motion naturalness or semantic responsiveness.

The individual ingredients build substantially on Self-Forcing, DMD, rolling KV caches, noisy history, and standard inference optimizations. The novelty lies mainly in their integration and timestep-pipelined deployment; claims that TPP is broadly model- and hardware-agnostic should be moderated because it requires causal generation, balanced timestep stages, enough devices, and favorable communication costs.

Reproducibility remains limited by training on 128 H800 GPUs and by the absence of an available project link, code, model weights, or benchmark at review time. The ethical statement also asserts that all identity data were collected with permission without explaining how this applies to AVSpeech or documenting consent and licensing for avatar-generation use.
